I do a lot of hiking, and I've been in the woods for most of my life. The dumbest thing I've ever seen is people who start up a 9 mile hike, in flip flops, at noon, with one water bottle between two people and no other equipment. That's how people get lost in the woods or get dehydrated and suffer. It's just so stupid. I hope they turn back before they get to the end, but for all I know they're dehydrated and climbing out of the woods at 8pm. I always feel for those people, but it's sondamn stupid.

Yikes. This was me and my parents on the first hike, of the first day, of the first trip we took to the Smoky Mountains. We had not very much water (but some), and we just threw on some shoes we had handy but they weren't particularly great. We encountered a group of hikers that knew what they were doing most of the way up, they handed us some of their water and told us (through their shocked faces) how much like n00bs we obviously were.

When we got down out of that trail, we went and got a backpack and some proper shoes for everybody that night, and tackled our next trail much better prepared.

That's a great learning experience. Maybe instead of judging, I should start doing that... I always bring too much water anyways. I feel weird doing that though because a lot of these people are older than I am (I'm 22, but I'm super short so I look younger), and I don't know how well it'll be taken.

When I was Senior Patrol Leader (boy scout in charge) on a climbing camping trip, one of my scouts decided it would be lots of fun to go to the top of an 80 foot rock formation, run up to a tree growing on the edge of said cliff, and give it a flying side kick. It was not that strong of a tree as evidenced that it made a cracking sound. The idiot was lucky he didn't fall.

Anyway, an adult leader yelled at him and then yelled at me to go yell at him some more. He was not allowed to climb on things for the rest of the trip.

This reminds me of a great story that my friend told me about when he was in scouts, that his troop leader would sum up in a particular tl;dr sort of way when they were all exchanging 'war stories' around the fires at Philmont later:

"Parents don't like it when they give you their kids, and you bring them back dead."

Out in NM, there are a lot of rock faces. So, this troop was going to take a trip to hike to the top of a cliff face and then climb down it. Maybe they were going to walk down the trail and then climb back up? I don't remember the exact details, but there were people at the top of the cliff at the start, this is important.

So, one bratty kid decides the cliffside is just too scary. He stays up top while everybody else gets set to go, and ultimately, while the kids are climbing he's doing stupid things like tossing small rocks over the edge at them and otherwise just being the kind of kid that talks a big game and then chickens out and insists he stay on top of the cliff during the climbing trip.

And then, he's running around up there, and slips. Ends up careening off the cliffside, screaming on his way down, past the rest of the troop that are climbing down the cliffside. Succumbed to his injuries down there, and didn't make it home.

My re-telling of the story makes it sound like he was up there all on his own with no supervision, but truth is I just don't know exactly what that situation was, whether there was somebody up there with him or not.

The age range for scouting fits well within the age range for thinking one is invincible. Even with supervision, the environments are those where stupidity is painful and extreme stupidity is fatal. I had the privilege of going to Philmont twice, and there were a lot of places where you just had to be mature and pay attention. No amount of supervision can compensate for lacking a basic level of maturity out in the back country. That's why they have age requirements for high adventures. Fortunately, none of our scouts ever died while out on a trip. A few hospital trips (allergies, whittling accident, etc.) were all we had to deal with when I was there.
